elements.text: Light control force characteristics of the MD-11 in high altitude cruise flight
Moderate lateral gust inducing the upset
Excessive control deflections exacerbating the upset
Lack of pilot training specific to recovery from high altitude, high speed upsets in the MD-11
Flightcrew was certificated and qualified
Airplane was certificated and maintained in accordance with regulations
Airplane was dispatched in accordance with procedures
No air traffic control factors in the cause
Airplane encountered moderate turbulence
Lateral gust initiated the upset (supported by FDR data)
Autopilot disengaged due to excessive roll rate during gust
Airplane stalled at least four times before recovery
Flightcrew reactions exacerbated the situation and led to pitch/airspeed deviations
Aft center-of-gravity position resulting in lower longitudinal stability margins
Lighter control forces compared to conventional transports leading to overcontrol
LSAS introducing nose-down pitching moment requiring heavy control force
Captain continued to exert back force maintaining stall condition
Stall buffet produced dynamic load causing structural overload and elevator failure
Elevator skin separation from overstress during stall buffet
Control not adversely affected by loss of outboard elevators
Douglas Aircraft did not demonstrate stall recovery from abrupt high altitude upsets
Pilots did not receive training for recovering from high altitude upsets
Pilots did not receive hands-on training for light control forces at high altitude/speed
Recommendations to FAA regarding Douglas Aircraft advisories
Recommendations to FAA regarding nondestructive inspection of elevators
Recommendations to FAA regarding certification requirements for flight control handling
Previous recommendations regarding simulator upgrades and training guidance

Previous recommendations regarding high altitude stall margins
